spot.title: A Laura-Sized Hole
spot.subtitle: The principal who held a famously progressive school district together

locating.anchor: the small cluster of school buildings set back from the road among the trees

document.text: The Lagunitas School District, based here in the valley, has long been one of the most progressive in California, home to Open Classroom, Montessori, and once a Waldorf-inspired program. The Point Reyes Light reported in twenty twenty-four on the retirement of Laura Shain, the principal who led the district for thirteen years, through the closure of the Waldorf program, a pandemic, and the difficult merger of the two remaining programs. In her first year she abolished dress code rules she considered sexist, and colleagues credited her with holding the community together through painful transitions. She left content. “The foundation has been built and the school will never stop changing, but we're just poised for more fine-tuning at this point.” Meegan Potter, a former school board member, put the loss simply. “We're losing such a legacy. There's a Laura-sized hole to replace and it's going to be very challenging.”

spot.title: Dogtown and the Thirteen Turns
spot.subtitle: An Irishman's boundary trees meet a three-and-a-half-million-dollar chainsaw

locating.anchor: the tall eucalyptus trees crowding the winding stretch of highway

document.text: This tiny settlement is Dogtown, and the winding stretch of highway near it is known to locals as the Thirteen Turns. The towering eucalyptus here were planted by Henry Strain, an Irish immigrant dairy farmer who used the trees to mark the boundaries of his Dogtown property; after his ranch ceased operating in the nineteen seventies, young eucalyptus spread across the old pastureland beside the road. The Point Reyes Light reported in twenty twenty-one that Caltrans had launched a three point five million dollar safety project to trim or remove up to two hundred of the aging trees along this highway. Not everyone was pleased. Bolinas resident Dale Polissar wrote to the paper in protest. “We who love that beautiful drive should have something to say about this, and maybe it's not too late to stop it—or at least moderate it.” Beauty, he argued, deserved a seat beside safety.

spot.title: Three Faults and a Flooded Road
spot.subtitle: Redesigning the lagoon's north end for the rising Pacific

locating.anchor: the junction where the lagoon's marshy north end meets the highway

document.text: At this junction, where the road to Bolinas splits away, the highway skirts the marshy north end of Bolinas Lagoon, a federally protected water body where winter storms regularly push floodwater over the pavement. The Point Reyes Light reported in twenty sixteen on county plans to remake this corner of the lagoon: three alternatives that ranged from restoring the floodplains of two creeks to lifting the highway onto causeways, and even decommissioning the Olema Bolinas Road entirely. County planner Veronica Pearson explained why nothing here is simple. “This is a really complex geologic area. There are three faults converging right at this location.” Two years later the paper reported that Caltrans was clearing culverts and ditches along the lagoon's eastern bank, after advisors warned that floodwaters washing over car undercarriages were rinsing petroleum and brake dust straight into the lagoon.

spot.title: A Billion-Dollar Line in the Sand
spot.subtitle: The most vulnerable town in Marin plans for the encroaching ocean

locating.anchor: the low-lying beach town clustered between the lagoon and the ocean

document.text: Stinson Beach, wedged between the Pacific and Bolinas Lagoon, is considered the most vulnerable coastal community in Marin County. The Point Reyes Light reported in twenty twenty-five on a fifty-six page blueprint laying out a one point two billion dollar strategy to help this town of about five hundred residents withstand the rising ocean, from elevating roads and restoring dunes to replacing septic systems. The projections were sobering: with three point three feet of sea-level rise, nearly all development on the ocean side of the highway falls within a flood hazard zone. James Jackson, a hydrologist on the study, described the bind. “There's no obvious site where the community could simply relocate. But it's hard to envision the community remaining exactly where it is after several feet of sea-level rise.” One longtime resident, Jeff Loomans, doubted the town could pull it off. “Stinson is an unincorporated village with no central political entity that could take the lead on this. Implementing this plan is a pipe dream.”

spot.title: Twenty-Two Acres of Sixth Graders
spot.subtitle: The valley's middle school since nineteen sixty-nine

locating.anchor: the low school buildings and playing fields on Glen Drive

document.text: The campus on Glen Drive is White Hill Middle School, named for the hill it sits beneath. It opened in nineteen sixty-nine on twenty-two acres at the western edge of Fairfax, surrounded by hills and open space, and it has been the single middle school for the Ross Valley School District ever since, drawing every sixth, seventh and eighth grader from Fairfax and San Anselmo. About six hundred twenty-eight students attend. The school has been rebuilt in stages, with major renovations in nineteen eighty-five, two thousand, and twenty thirteen, when twenty-five thousand square feet of new classrooms opened. Like most Marin districts it leans on a local parcel tax, and in twenty twenty-six voters were asked to renew and raise it under Measure H, to one thousand two hundred eighty-two dollars per parcel, which the campaign noted is the lowest rate among Marin's kindergarten-through-eighth districts. The money goes to teachers and class sizes, not buildings. If you are driving through at three in the afternoon, expect bicycles.

spot.title: Half a Mile of Liability
spot.subtitle: The evacuation road that floods at king tides, and the fight over who pays

locating.anchor: the two-lane road heading out toward the Seadrift gate

document.text: The side road here is Calle del Arroyo, a county-owned two-lane street that runs half a mile from the highway to the Seadrift gate. It is the only way in or out for about five hundred homes, and it is their tsunami evacuation route. It is also already impassable during the annual king tides, and flooded again in January of twenty twenty-six. County planners expect it to flood in major storms by around twenty fifty and at ordinary monthly high tides sometime between twenty sixty and twenty seventy-five. Raising and fortifying it carries a preliminary price tag of twenty-two point eight million dollars, with the work spread across two decades. When a draft county document suggested Marin might not be required to maintain access if coastal hazards made it infeasible, the Seadrift Association answered with a warning of billions in liability. The county withdrew the language. The water is still coming.

spot.title: Trail Bikes and the Mount Tam Watershed Plan
spot.subtitle: Point Reyes Light · 2026-09-02

document.text: The trails above Fairfax are the subject of a new access debate. In the September second, twenty twenty-six Point Reyes Light, Ben Stocking reports that Marin Water proposes recognizing twenty-seven miles of previously unsanctioned bike trails. Most would be shared; two would be downhill bike routes. This was a proposal undergoing environmental review, not permission to ride every single-track trail. Horse riders worried about losing historic access and about speed differences. Supporters pointed to riders who use pedal assistance to keep riding into old age. Conservation League member Larry Minikes put the practical question plainly: “It's great to have these plans but only if there's accountability and funding behind them.” The article announced a September tenth scoping meeting at Sky Oaks. The larger story is about maintenance as much as access: drainage, erosion, ranger staffing, and the money needed to keep a shared trail usable. A line drawn on a map does not maintain itself.

spot.title: Lagunitas Creek: A Messy Creek Is a Happy Creek
spot.subtitle: Point Reyes Light · 2026-09-02

document.text: A fallen tree in Lagunitas Creek can look like a maintenance problem. For young salmon, it can be shelter. Ara Rosenthal's September second, twenty twenty-six Light report follows Sarah Phillips, who helps creekside property owners through Marin's Urban Streams Coordination Program. The county renewed the program with a five-year, one-and-a-half-million-dollar contract. Phillips visits sites, explains permits, and connects residents with specialists. Her phrase is worth remembering: “But a messy creek is a happy creek.” Wood can slow currents, create pools, shade the water, and support insects that fish eat. That does not mean every fallen tree is harmless; the program assesses individual situations. It also helps people protect threatened structures without automatically covering banks in rock. The useful change in thinking is visible from any creek crossing along this road. A tidy channel and a healthy channel are not necessarily the same thing. Sometimes restoration means learning which apparent messes to leave alone.

spot.title: Bears on Coast and Sky Trails: The 2026 Evidence
spot.subtitle: Point Reyes Light · 2026-09-02

document.text: Black bears have been reported along Coast and Sky Trails, the very trail network ahead. Ben Stocking's September second, twenty twenty-six Light article describes a more careful way to understand those reports: cameras and DNA from scat. Inverness wildlife photographer Sarah Killingsworth collects samples for the North Bay Bear Collaborative. She had gathered fifteen samples the previous year, with analysis underway at U.C. Davis. Fifteen samples do not mean fifteen bears. One animal can leave evidence at several locations and cross county lines. Killingsworth's estimate of as many as ten Marin bears remained an estimate, not a completed census. After installing cameras in the seashore, she recorded seven bear appearances, again without claiming seven different animals. Asked about coexistence, Meghan Walla-Murphy said, “Their whole movement is determined by their bellies, which informs their noses.” The story connects this forest to a much wider landscape. An animal passing across a trail is also passing through the limits of what researchers currently know.

spot.title: Olema and the Coast: Measuring Fog in 2026
spot.subtitle: Point Reyes Light · 2026-08-26

document.text: The temperature change between Olema and the coast now has measuring equipment behind it. Lisa Krieger reported in the August twenty-sixth, twenty twenty-six Light that researchers installed matching fog collectors at the former G Ranch near the ocean and at the Point Reyes Field Station in Olema Valley. Mesh catches droplets, which drain through gauges. The sites belong to a five-year coastal research project. On June tenth the coastal collector gathered three liters of moisture, while the inland station recorded only trace amounts. That is a measurement at an instrument, not the total water delivered to a whole ranch. Researcher Dan Fernandez described why fog is difficult to count: “You have droplets forming; you have droplets evaporating. Droplets change in size and numbers.” The team is investigating where fog forms and how much water it delivers, with climate trends still unresolved. Along Limantour Road, the change in vegetation becomes a way to notice the question being measured.

spot.title: Tomales Bay: Two Paddlers Lost in August 2026
spot.subtitle: Point Reyes Light · 2026-09-02

document.text: The September second, twenty twenty-six Light carried a serious Tomales Bay story. Two men, Casey Flynn Melia and Alexander Ferguson, did not return from a late-night paddle to see bioluminescence. Their group had been camping at White Gulch Beach. Searchers found the men in different parts of the northern bay. Both had been wearing lifejackets. The cause and manner of death were still under investigation when Ben Stocking reported the story. Local outfitter Liz Wilhelm said, “Any amount of time in the water can be dangerous.” The article described cold water, wind, and currents, and emphasized that the bay's luminous nighttime display occurs in an exposed marine environment. It was the second fatal canoe incident reported on the bay that year. The locations of the recoveries are farther north than Inverness; this is a bay-community story, not a claim that the incident happened beside the town. It gives the beautiful water outside the windows a very immediate human context.

Ben Stocking reported in the September second, twenty twenty-six Light that Marin County Free Library had joined Dolly Parton's Imagination Library that summer. Eligible children receive a free book in the mail each month, from birth through age five. The article counted thirteen hundred Marin participants, with many more eligible. Library director Lana Adlawan emphasized the pleasure of receiving something addressed to the child and building a home collection. Parton's remark, quoted in the story, is concise: “If I'm remembered 100 years from now, I hope it will be not for looks, but for books.” The program uses age-matched selections, including sturdy books for babies, and offers English and Spanish selections. This spot belongs across Point Reyes Station rather than at one doorway, because its subject is a service reaching homes throughout the community. A small monthly delivery can become one of a child's first regular encounters with reading.

spot.subtitle: Point Reyes Light · 2026-09-02

document.text: An outdoor stage at St. Columba's brings seventeenth-century French comedy into an Inverness weekend. Ben Stocking's September second, twenty twenty-six Light article describes Geoff Hoyle's adaptation of Molière's final play, The Imaginary Invalid. The production was called Sick to Death, presented by Sharron Drake Community Arts. Hoyle translated the language for contemporary actors and added some material of his own. He saw parallels between the play's medical salesmen and modern wellness businesses, but said, “I wanted people to draw their own parallels and conclusions.” Hoyle's stage career included playing Zazu in the original Broadway Lion King. Here the setting was the church's outdoor theater, with a cast mixing professional experience and community participation. The performances announced in the article belong to early September twenty twenty-six. The enduring local subject is that a small town can sustain ambitious theater, with translation, rehearsal and an audience gathered outside rather than in a large metropolitan playhouse.

document.text: For Muir Beach, another hundred dollars per parcel became an investment in emergency response. The Point Reyes Light reported on June 17, 2026, that voters had approved Measure M, renewing the community’s fire protection tax. The annual rate rose from 286 to 386 dollars per parcel. County election materials specified a ten-year term, with possible annual inflation adjustments, supporting firehouse maintenance, emergency preparedness and equipment upgrades. As this drive reaches the coastal community, that vote offers a glimpse of the local financing behind its fire service: a tax expected to raise about 61,000 dollars annually.
